There is, then, something like a tremendous upward surge of being, rising from the depths of inorganic existence to the emergence of earthly human form, and going still further beyond it. For the human being, as he exists in this world, is still a being in between.

We must not misunderstand this: Mulla Sadra’s vision reaches far beyond, and moves in quite another direction from, the evolutionism that has become a dogma in the West. In that doctrine everything unfolds along a horizontal line, on one and the same level of being. People speak endlessly and carelessly of the “meaning of history,” forgetting that to speak of such a meaning one must at least possess an eschatology—a vision of ultimate destiny.

The movement of Mulla Sadra’s universe, like that of all the thinkers we are considering, is not the movement of a world evolving but of a world ascending. Its orientation is vertical, Gothic in style, we might say. It corresponds to the Mabda' and the Ma'ad, the Origin and the Return, through which metahistory—the dimension of reality beyond ordinary historical time—breaks into our world.

This irruption of metahistory, together with our example of the body and the metamorphoses through which it takes part in being’s upward movement, gives us what we need to suggest how profoundly Mulla Sadra’s “existential” metaphysics differs from contemporary “existentialism.” Elsewhere we have examined at greater length the texts in which Sadra’s concept of existence becomes clear as a concept of Presence, so that the degree of the act of being, or existing (wujud), is defined in terms of Presence (huzur).

As our shaykh explains, the astronomical heavens, for instance, are not present to the Earth considered as a physical mass. Nothing belonging to the world of phenomena—matter, extension, bodily volume, spatial distance—can be present to anything else in this sense. A being is present to itself, is present to another, and can have another present to it—indeed, there can be any such presence at all—only to the extent that the being becomes “separated” (tajrid) from the conditions of this world, which is subject to extension, volume, distance, and chronological time.

The more completely it frees itself from those conditions, the further it moves from what makes absence, concealment, and death possible. It is therefore also increasingly freed from the conditions of a being destined to end, a “being-toward-death.” For Mulla Sadra and all the Ishraqiyun, the more intense the degree of Presence, the more intense the act of existing. And the more fully this existence is an act of being that extends beyond death, the more fully the being makes up its “lag” (ta'akkhor) behind total Presence. Our shaykh’s entire philosophy of Resurrection develops this fundamental insight.

Because his metaphysics of being is an “existential” metaphysics that gives existence priority over essence, it culminates in Presence, which is itself the act of being of a spiritual being. (A thing is not “present” to another thing.) Because this metaphysics has no agnostic reflex that would rule out knowledge of spiritual realities, and because it conceives of being as an ordered hierarchy of many levels and worlds, its idea of Presence cannot possibly privilege “presence in this world.”

Quite the opposite: it liberates the human being from this world, since this world is incompatible with the act of true Presence. Presence, as Mulla Sadra understands it, is certainly a presence that is “committed,” to use a fashionable word.

But it is committed, here and now, beyond death and on the far side of death, to a destiny after earthly life—the destiny we shall discuss later, and one it is much less fashionable to speak about today. Such Presence cannot be ensnared by the apparent history of this world, because commitment in the fullest and truest sense can only be to what belongs to metahistory.

A being can undertake that commitment only when its “polar dimension” is revealed to it; and that revelation already makes its act of existing an act of presence to the worlds beyond death. Nor does our existence in this world emerge from some preceding nothingness. Sadra expressly invokes the passage in which Ibn Babuyeh affirms the general Shiite belief in preexistence—the preexistence of Spirits before bodies.

The scale of being, and the reach of the many forms of Presence embraced by “knowledge through presence” ('ilm huzuri), cannot be measured by the same standards in this traditional metaphysics as in a philosophy paralyzed by agnosticism. To Mulla Sadra, the assumptions of the latter philosophy could only deepen a being’s “lag,” compelling it to remain behind itself. We are clearly far from what is called “existentialism” today.

Are there philosophical arguments we might exchange in order to convince one another about such matters? We hardly think so. These are things given in immediate experience: either one perceives them or one does not. No dialectical argument can change that, and phenomenological analysis must be all the more attentive to them.

The idea of Presence, as we have said, implies that of a witness, a shahid. An eyewitness is someone who is “present to” something, who sees directly. Suhrawardi had already maintained that if we trust the testimony of observations made by Hipparchus and Ptolemy in astronomy, we should also trust the testimony of those who have entered the Malakut, the spiritual world.

In Mulla Sadra, the metaphysics of Presence develops into a metaphysics of witnessing, culminating in the doctrine of the Imams at the summit of prophetic philosophy. The spiritual understanding of the Imams is, above all, a theosophy founded on testimony and witnessing. We have already glimpsed this summit (Book I, chapter VII, § 4). Here it will be enough to recall the ways in which Mulla Sadra leads us toward it.

One of the most important titles the hadith give the Twelve Imams is “Witnesses of God.” In that capacity, each of the Twelve has a twofold role: toward God, to whom he is present and who is present through him to human beings; and toward human beings, to whom God is present through him and who, through him, are present to God.

Existence understood as Presence, and Presence understood as a union of a special kind between the knower and what is known—this is the insight that allows Mulla Sadra to penetrate the meaning of the Imam’s simultaneous presence in both directions. It allows him to place Shiite teaching about the Imams, and the persons of the Twelve Imams themselves, not merely on the level of their earthly appearance and historical lives but on the level of their metaphysical reality as God’s eternal Witnesses.

The metaphysics of Presence unfolds into a metaphysics of the witness borne by God’s Witnesses: those who are present to God and through whom God is present to humanity and humanity is present to God. The very idea of walayat traces out and completes this circle. This is what gives full meaning to the saying: “Whoever dies without knowing his Imam dies the death of those who remain unaware.”

It is in the same capacity that the Imams are also called both the Treasurers and the Treasures of divine knowledge: they are at once the medium and the object of God’s own knowing. For everything the Divine Being knows is known through its knowledge of itself—in an act of self-knowledge. What the Divine Being knows in this way are the forms of beings. Just as it knows the beings of the cosmic creation through their Angels, so it knows, through the Imams and the awliya, the beings who are accomplishing their Return toward it. This parallel is essential.

The gnostic’s ('arif’s) knowledge of the Imam is not simply knowledge of his outward person as he appears in physical form; anyone can know him in that way. Truly to know the Imam is to be present to the Imam’s Presence as Witness of God. The Presence of this Witness to God means God’s Presence to itself in that eternal Adam, in the hidden, inner reality of the “Muhammadan Reality” that is the primordial theophany, the first divine self-disclosure. This self-presence is, by that very fact, the emergence of manifested being on the spiritual plane.

To be present to the Imam is therefore to be present, through him, to the God to whom the Imam himself is present as Witness; and through this same Witness, God is present to everyone who is present to the Witness and to whom the Witness is present.

If we fail to understand that it is through and within this Witness that Deus absconditus, the hidden God, becomes Deus revelatus, the revealed God—if, in other words, we do not understand that this Witness, the Imam, provides both the form and the content of all human knowledge of God—then monotheism, reduced to an abstraction, falls into the trap of metaphysical idolatry. It confuses the Witness with the One on whose behalf the Witness testifies and to whom he answers: the One who can be reached only through the testimony he gives to himself within this Witness.

We can now understand how, through this reciprocity of Presences, the Imam becomes, in Mulla Sadra’s spirituality, the inner Witness and Guide (Hujjat batina). This is why we have already seen the famous saying, “Whoever knows himself knows his Lord,” overlaid, as though in a transparent image, by another: “Whoever knows his Imam knows his Lord.”

The mysticism of Najm Kobra, for its part, introduced us to the inner master, the invisible Guide (shaykh al-ghayb, ostad ghaybi). And Semnani’s way of reading sacred texts, together with his vocabulary, had already led us to speak of “the Imam of your being.” In doing so, we were anticipating what the doctrine of the Imams now shows us: how that very doctrine contains the foundation and the secret of its own inward realization.

The profound link between Mulla Sadra’s prophetic philosophy and Shiite spirituality thus comes into view. The Ishraqi metaphysics of Presence culminates in a metaphysics of the Imamate as divine Presence to the human being, who is himself present to his inner Witness and Guide. The Imams, as Witnesses, are that Presence.
We shall see later how Qazi Sa'id Qommi arrives at a closely similar analysis by taking up another theme furnished by the hadith.

A few pages ago we said that from the doctrine of the Imams, at the summit of prophetic philosophy, we could glimpse a continuous path leading to a metaphysics of Resurrection. We have now learned that the Imam is the Witness whom God beholds and through whom he beholds: God knows the believer through that believer’s “inner Imam.” Through the Imams he knows and looks upon the beings who are making their Return toward him.

But this Return is precisely the upward surge of being, the restlessness that sets beings in motion at every level of its hierarchy. Mulla Sadra seeks to account for this movement through his “existential” metaphysics, in which the act of being of each creature opens into a cycle of metamorphoses. The present “cycle of walayat,” whose place in the prophetic philosophy of Shiism we have just recalled, marks the phase of this Return corresponding to humanity’s present condition.

Since the Imam is the Perfect Human Being (al-Insan al-kamil), Adam in the true sense, the metaphysical Adam (Adam al-haqiqi), we can discern a connection between the doctrine of the Imams and the understanding of humanity of which that doctrine is the supreme expression. The philosophy of Resurrection discloses precisely the secret, the inner meaning, of that connection. Its nature and significance will have to be developed in future research.

Here we wish only to sketch the metaphysics of Resurrection as it emerges from the masterly glosses Mulla Sadra wrote in the margins of Suhrawardi’s Eastern Theosophy. Alongside the fundamental principles of his metaphysics of being, this metaphysics of Resurrection brings into play two further defining doctrines of Sadra Shirazi: one concerning active Imagination, the other the imaginal world.

Mulla Sadra’s collected glosses on Suhrawardi’s Book of Eastern Theosophy form a substantial work: in a typeset edition they would fill a hefty volume of some six hundred pages. The modest title should not mislead us. Under the name of glosses, scholia, or marginal annotations (hashiyat, ta'liqat), Sadra Shirazi has in fact produced a monumental and deeply personal work.

Some of these glosses occupy only a few lines; others have the scope and weight of complete lectures, in which the commentator examines Suhrawardi’s text in depth, almost always striving to establish his own position. His response ranges through every shade, from admiring agreement to reservation and criticism. Perhaps what we possess here are the texts of lectures Mulla Sadra delivered either during his years in Shiraz or even earlier.

These glosses begin with the first book of the first part of the work by the Shaykh al-Ishraq, the Master of Illumination, and continue to the end of the fifth and final book of its second part. Elsewhere we have expressed the hope that a critical edition will soon appear, and described the form in which the glosses are preserved in the only lithographed edition so far published.

I shall recall only that, when working particularly closely on the glosses to the second part—the characteristic portion of Suhrawardi’s book—I found it necessary, for ease of reference, to count them and give them consecutive numbers from beginning to end. I arrived at a total of six hundred and forty-six glosses across both parts, allowing for a possible margin of error, though it should not amount to more than a few.

Whenever a gloss is numbered in the pages that follow, that number refers to my sequence. We also give the corresponding page in the old lithographed edition and, where appropriate, the page of Suhrawardi’s own text in our edition, identified by the initials H.I. All the glosses we discuss here concern Book V of the second part of Eastern Theosophy, the book devoted above all to the last things and to resurrection.
We shall follow these glosses as one follows a rhapsody, for a rhapsody rather than a systematic construction is what they are.

Yet the teachings of the master of Shiraz grow and deepen, taking on the themes closest to his heart as Suhrawardi’s text calls them forth. At the beginning of Book V, that text first confronts him with the question of transmigration (tanasukh): the passage of a soul from one body to another. Mulla Sadra will explain in what sense he finds transmigration inconceivable, and how we might interpret the ancient sages, including Pythagoras and Plato, who upheld it.

But a more pressing problem takes hold of him. The Muslim thinkers who preceded him seem to have left Mulla Sadra with a choice. Either resurrection is understood as ma'ad jismani, a bodily resurrection, taken by literalist theologians to mean the material restoration of the elemental, physical body; or it is understood with the philosophers of the Avicennian school as ma'ad ruhani, a resurrection that is purely spiritual.

We shall see Mulla Sadra reject this dilemma and dismiss the theologians and philosophers alike—Ghazali no less than Avicenna—while explaining why both have failed to develop a genuine “philosophy of Resurrection.” What they lacked was an account of the reality of the interworld, the realm between the sensible and the intelligible that Suhrawardi was the first to give a place within a philosophical scheme. They lacked, in fact, the faculty through which that interworld can be grasped and understood: active Imagination, whose irreplaceable power of knowledge Ibn Arabi demonstrates again and again.

Consequently, neither side could conceive what the “body of resurrection” truly is: the acquired body (jism muktasab), shaped by the human being’s spiritual powers in their own image, the caro spiritualis, or spiritual flesh. Ibn Arabi’s writings therefore assume a particularly important place in Mulla Sadra’s treatment of the question.

Throughout the movements of his thought, however, Mulla Sadra remains faithful to a golden rule, which, as we have seen, he explains admirably in the prologue to his great commentary on Book III of Kolayni’s collection, the Kitab al-Hujja. The hadith in that book deal especially with the understanding of prophecy and the Imams in Shiism. It is above all when they address a subject such as resurrection that Mulla Sadra and his fellow thinkers show how foreign to them is the disastrous separation of philosophy from theology that goes back, in the West, to the age of medieval scholasticism.

For Quranic Revelation and philosophical knowledge are inseparable from a standpoint that rises above the level at which we are accustomed to separate theology from philosophy. That higher standpoint joins them together and is called 'irfan, or mystical theosophy—the wisdom of spiritual knowledge. We have already heard Mulla Sadra state in strikingly concise terms the metaphysical law that makes the two inseparable at this higher level: divine Revelation is the light that makes seeing possible; the philosopher’s meditation is the light that sees.

To dispense with the former, as certain extreme Mu'tazilites do, is to wander in the night. To dispense with the latter, in the devout agnosticism of the literalists, is to remain blind. 'Irfan, mystical theosophy, is “Light upon Light.” That is why not even the shadow of the Latin Averroist idea of “double truth” can arise here.

Whoever perceives the different levels of being can perceive, at the level proper to it, a spiritual truth that is, on that very level, the literal truth of eschatology: the truth of the Quran and of the hadith of the Prophet and the holy Imams alike. And Mulla Sadra says explicitly that this was the distinctive spiritual gift of Shiite theosophy within Islam. There is still much in this teaching for us to explore.

A dozen or so glosses at the opening of Book V already reveal the direction of Mulla Sadra’s thought and lead toward a common goal. Above all, they represent his effort to establish the reality of the interworld and to show how it stands in symbolic correspondence with both the sensible and the intelligible universes. Everything depends on this account of reality if the passages of divine Revelation concerning the last things are to be understood in their spiritual truth (haqiqat).

Yet that spiritual truth, when perceived by the faculty suited to the level of being to which the divine indications refer, is at the same time both symbolic and literal truth. The function of a symbol must never be confused with that of an allegory, as so often happens. We have had occasion to insist on this many times. Allegory remains on the same plane of being and evidence as ordinary perception.

Allegorical interpretation drains visionary events of their life and distorts them because it cannot, in fact, comprehend the reality of any events other than those perceived by the senses. Such interpretation is characteristic of rationalist thinkers, including extreme Mu'tazilites. Literalist theologians, for their part, reveal the same inability to rise to a higher level of perception. If allegorism is a flight from reality, literalism is a fall into absurdity.
Yet it sometimes happens that, through mere habit, people call an interpretation “allegorical” when it possesses all the qualities and merits of genuine symbolic interpretation.

Gloss no. 567 in our continuous numbering provides an extensive “introductory lesson” to Book V of the second part of Suhrawardi’s Book of Eastern Theosophy. It prepares the ground for a teaching on the imaginative faculty in relation to resurrection. Its necessary counterpart is the existence of the mundus imaginalis, the imaginal world, as a real interworld governed by laws of its own: a world whose reality is perceived specifically by the imaginative faculty.

The initial problem can be summed up in a question: How are we to understand all the Quran’s teachings about the world to come—paradise and hell, and, in short, the very idea of ma'ad jismani, bodily resurrection—without falling either into the literalism of theologians who are not philosophers or into the allegorism of rationalist philosophers? Mulla Sadra’s chief effort will be to distinguish tanasukh, transmigration, from ma'ad, literally the “Return,” as these two ideas are ordinarily understood, and then to show how the Return must be understood if even the idea of transmigration is to acquire a new and true meaning.

Our shaykh rejects tanasukh when it means the “pouring” of a spiritual entity out of one body and into another. He finds that idea as childish as the literalist theologians’ conception of the Return. One way of understanding the soul’s journey is to see human form as the “first threshold” through which the Soul passes as it descends into the world of Matter. On that account, should the Soul fail to fulfill the meaning of its earthly existence, it falls still further into the circles of lower creation.

Mulla Sadra takes the opposite view. For him, human form is the highest earthly limit of the Soul’s ascent from the deepest abyss. Human form is thus the threshold of the Malakut, the spiritual world. Here, the meaning of the last things and the very idea of resurrection clearly depend on a gnostic account of the Soul’s history—a spiritual drama whose details remain to be studied across the whole of Mulla Sadra’s work.

In the gloss under discussion, the argument begins by drawing, for the moment only, on the Peripatetic theory that things are composed of matter and form—hylomorphism. In that theory, each kind of matter actually exists by virtue of the Form that makes it actual. Conversely, each Form exists through and for the matter that it brings into actuality. Under Peripatetic assumptions, it is unthinkable that either should continue to exist independently of the other.

We must remember, however, that the Platonism already present in Avicenna’s doctrine prevented him from fully accepting the Peripatetic definition of the Soul as the form, or entelechy (perfection), of an organic body possessing life only potentially. For the Soul is, first of all, a spiritual being sufficient unto itself. Mulla Sadra therefore holds that a Form can possess, not merely as the form of an organic body but in itself, a perfection and a way of being fully actual by which it exists independently of all matter. More precisely, it becomes the very matter of the forms and images it itself brings into actuality.

But precisely in this case, because the Soul—the Espahbad Light—was temporarily united with the material body it had to govern, a certain way of being a soul has been actualized within it. Certain perfections of its being as a soul, affecting its deepest being, its very substance (istikmalat jawhariyya), have become actual through its use of an earthly human body as an instrument.

To take the idea of tanasukh literally, then, we would have to imagine that a soul which has already become an actual human soul could return to a state of mere potentiality in relation to an earthly human body—and thus become once again a human soul only in potential.
It would follow that a Form, once it had become actual, could return to being merely potential; that a soul which had become actual could become a soul in potential again. This is unacceptable.

The idea of maʿād—resurrection, or the return to life beyond death—does not present this difficulty, provided we do not imagine it as the soul's “return” to a physical organism reconstructed independently of it. That would simply bring us back to a variation on tanāsukh, the transmigration of souls.

No: the resurrection body (the body of the world beyond, jism ukhrāwī) is a body that the soul has formed for itself. It is the body the soul has acquired (jism muktasab) through its activity, its love, its conduct, and its habits, whether good or bad. “This acquired body stands in the same relation to the soul as a shadow to that which casts it.” (We should compare this with Semnānī's doctrine, discussed above in Book IV, Chapter IV, §5.)

To understand maʿād in its true sense, and therefore to see how it differs from tanāsukh, we must set aside every image of a physical transfer from one place to another—as though the soul left one material body only to enter another waiting to receive it.

We must think instead of a passage from one mode of being to another: for example, the passage from the intellectus materialis, or potential intellect, to intellect and intelligible reality in actuality.
We thus arrive at the notion of a “transfer in substance” (intiqāl jawharī), which is also a metamorphosis: the “acquired body” represents the new mode of being into which the soul has passed.

We must conceive of an unbroken process of renewal (ittiṣāl tajaddudī), an uninterrupted succession of transformations of being (akwān ittiṣālīya). We might say that the true idea of maʿād replaces transmigration with transubstantiation, and the passage of a soul from body to body (tanāsukh) with metamorphosis. The picture of a soul being poured from one vessel into another—of a “transfer in place”—leads to insurmountable difficulties.

But a progression from imperfection toward perfection, from lesser to greater intensity, from this world to another world, is not only possible: it expresses a truth that can be realized and verified through experience (mutaḥaqqaq). This ascent of the human being, degree by degree and world by world, will reappear later (Glosses 610, 620, and 629) as a foundation of Mullā Ṣadrā's thought. It also reveals his kinship with the Neoplatonic theosophers of the West since the Renaissance.

Mullā Ṣadrā's understanding of the human being also has a profound affinity with Ismaili gnosis. Through its conduct, habits, and actions, every soul brings into actuality a mode of being—an independent act of existence (wujūd istiqlālī)—that survives the dissolution and disappearance of the material body. This mode of being, the body the soul has acquired, gives it a hidden kinship of nature (munāsabat fī'l-bāṭin) with one of four kinds of beings: angel, demon, animal, or wild beast.

The soul becomes a being of one of these kinds, existing as a pure Form, independently of any matter that would receive it passively. Or rather, as we recalled earlier, the soul itself is now the “matter” of the Forms brought into actuality within it.

Our shaykh even suggests that this may be the key to understanding what Plato and his predecessors meant when they spoke of souls passing into the bodies of animals whose nature resembled their own. Their words are to be understood as symbols of a “second birth” or “second growth” (nashʾat thāniya), taking place in the world beyond, not in this world (see below, Gloss 629, on the three stages of human growth). The same applies to Qur'anic verses sometimes interpreted as teaching tanāsukh (41:20; 24:24; 6:38; 5:65; 17:99, among others), and to all the other symbolic figures found in the hadith.

If, then, we understand this passage as taking place in the world beyond rather than here below, and as a transformation in the mode of being—a “transfer in substance” (intiqāl jawharī) that becomes the acquired body (jism muktasab), not a movement from one physical place to another—we begin to see how transmigration, understood now as transubstantiation, converges with resurrection (maʿād). Both are being understood in their true sense. That is why, Mullā Ṣadrā observes, it has been said that there is no religious doctrine in which the idea of tanāsukh is not rooted.

But for that to be possible, our picture of the world must include a plane of being on which this event is literally true—not, of course, in the sense in which a physical event is literally true. Here the philosophers reveal their limitations.

“What astonishes me,” declares Mullā Ṣadrā, “is that Avicenna, with all the power of his genius, came to recognize that the hidden meaning of the transmigration (tanāsukh) spoken of by the Pillars of Wisdom—Plato, the Pythagoreans, the disciples of Buzurgmihr—lies in symbols (rumūz) and parables (tamthīlāt) of the prophetic teaching; and yet he was unable to resolve the problem of tanāsukh by an analysis that disclosed its true meaning (ʿalā'l-taḥqīq).

“He could not do so because he had not grasped the authentic meaning of bodily resurrection (maʿād jismānī) in a way that satisfied both philosophy (ḥikmat) and religious law and theology (sharīʿat).” Mullā Ṣadrā immediately explains why Avicenna failed to reach this understanding and therefore had to stop at the idea of a purely spiritual (maʿnawī) resurrection.

What strikes us most in a passage from Avicenna's treatise on resurrection, the Risālat al-Aḍḥawīya, is the repeated expression as if. His entire account of the human being's destiny after death is cast as a philosophy of as if. Speaking of the vicious qualities that remain in souls after the death of the body, and that themselves constitute their punishment, Avicenna says it is as if these souls (kaʾannahā) were still in material bodies after death.

The soul's presence in the body does not mean that it is mixed with the body, or simply placed alongside it; rather, the soul receives certain effects produced by the bodily faculties, while being able to act only upon its own body. This creates a double obstacle to the soul's attaining its proper perfection, or even becoming aware of the desire and delight that belong to its own nature. If it has not overcome this condition, the condition remains within it after death.

We can then say it is as if the soul were still in a body; as if the effects surrounding it took the form of animal bodies or savage beasts; as if a soul corrupted by vice had been placed, after death, in a body corresponding to those vices.

Unfortunately, piling up these instances of “as if” is not enough—indeed, does not even lead toward—the recognition of a body that is wholly real without being a material body of the physical, elemental world. Mullā Ṣadrā concludes: “This is the furthest a philosopher can go if he does not acknowledge the existence of another bodily world, distinct from our material and physical world.”

To understand bodily resurrection in its true sense, then, we must establish the existence of what Mullā Ṣadrā elsewhere calls “subtle spiritual matter” (mādda rūḥānīya laṭīfa). The expression corresponds to spissitudo spiritualis—spiritual density or substantiality—used by the seventeenth-century Cambridge Platonist Henry More. It also recalls Geistleiblichkeit, “spiritual embodiment,” a favorite theme of the well-known Swabian theosopher F. C. Oetinger, a follower of Boehme and Swedenborg in the eighteenth century. Alongside this, we need a cosmology with room for the realm of subtle bodies: the intermediate world (al-ʿālam al-awsaṭ), the celestial Earth in which lie the mystical cities of Jābalqā, Jābarsā, and Hūrqalyā.

Suhrawardī was the first to define, in philosophical terms, the function of this intermediate world, an indispensable part of the cosmology and eschatology of the “Oriental Theosophy.” It is not the world of Platonic Ideas (muthul Iflāṭūnīya), but a world of substantial, self-subsisting Forms and Images, described as “suspended” (muʿallaqa).

This technical term means that they have no material substrate (lā fī maḥall) in which they inhere, as an accidental quality inheres in a material body—for instance, blackness in a black object. They subsist like images in a mirror: the substance of the mirror is not the material substrate of the image. This world partakes of both the intelligible and the sensible. Its own organ of perception is the imaginative faculty. It is the mundus imaginalis, the imaginal world (ʿālam al-Mithāl).

In Gloss 567, which we have just examined and discussed, Mullā Ṣadrā opens his commentary on Book V of the Oriental Theosophy with something like a master class. All the great themes are already present. And already his attitude toward the Shaykh al-Ishrāq, the Master of Illumination, begins to show its complexity. He ends this lesson by expressing a further surprise: Suhrawardī, who so convincingly established the existence and necessity of the intermediate world—the subtle world of Image and Imaginal reality—does not seem to understand the hidden meaning of the ancient sages' tanāsukh in quite the way Mullā Ṣadrā does.
Yet we have the impression that Ṣadrā finds in Suhrawardī an interpretation very close to his own.
To decide the matter, we would have to follow Suhrawardī's text and Mullā Ṣadrā's explanations closely, step by step. We cannot do that here.

But this opening lesson will help us understand the later Glosses on which we particularly wish to dwell. Above all, there is Gloss 616, where Mullā Ṣadrā perceptively reveals the organic connection between his philosophy of resurrection and the whole of his theosophy.
We will encounter Avicenna's position again, already clearly placed in perspective here.

We will also see the way prepared for another major Gloss, Gloss 629, in which Mullā Ṣadrā describes the human being's destiny after death through the threefold structure of human nature: physical human, psychic human, and spiritual human (jism, nafs, rūḥ—body, soul, spirit). This same triad is fundamental to Christian Gnosis (sōma or sarx, psychē, pneuma), though it was abandoned by official Christian anthropology at the Second Council of Constantinople, in 869 CE.

One thesis will gradually become clearer and more emphatic, a thesis on which, for Mullā Ṣadrā, everything else depends: the active Imagination, the power that forms images, is not an organic faculty bound to the material body and perishing with it, as so many philosophers have taught. It is a spiritual faculty that the soul “takes with it”; this image-forming power is the soul's subtle or imaginal body.
Hence Mullā Ṣadrā's particular eagerness to draw on Ibn ʿArabī at this point.

Let us note a few striking statements from the Glosses that prepare us for this conclusion. In Gloss 589 (Tehran lithograph, p. 491), itself an extensive lesson, Mullā Ṣadrā remarks, in a passage whose full context we cannot examine here: “If by tajarrud [separation from matter] one means separation from subtle bodies (ajsām mithālīya) as well as from sensible bodies, then this cannot hold for any souls except those who have attained perfection in gnosis and moral practice. If one means separation from the sensible material body but not from the subtle body, then the opinion is sound.

“For we have demonstrated elsewhere, by conclusive proof, that the imaginative and representational faculty (mutakhayyila) is independent of the physical body and separable from it and from the physical world. Once it has left this world, therefore, the soul still perceives individual things and still possesses conscious senses: hearing, sight, smell, taste, and touch. It also possesses a faculty of movement.

“Yet all these powers can be reduced to a single faculty: the active Imagination. For the external sensory faculties are all shadows and traces of the inner faculties, and all those inner faculties return to the soul's essential center—to the soul itself.”

In another context (Gloss 592, lithograph, p. 493), while discussing the different ways Alexander of Aphrodisias, Themistius, and Avicenna interpreted Aristotle, Mullā Ṣadrā declares emphatically: “There are imperfect souls that have failed to attain the perfection of intelligible knowledge; there are also souls that have taken on the shape of erroneous beliefs. To decide that all such souls perish is a position born of utter ignorance of two things: (1) that the imaginative power is purely spiritual (tajarrud al-quwwat al-mutakhayyila); and (2) that there exists an intermediate world between the sensible and intelligible worlds”—the ʿālam al-Mithāl, the imaginal world already mentioned above.

We must therefore affirm, with Suhrawardī, that “spiritual entities (mujarradāt) are indestructible, and that they differ from one another spiritually: through each one's consciousness of itself, through their lights and illuminations (ishrāqāt), and through the individuality proper to each, which arises from the way it governs the fortress of its body” (Ḥikmat al-Ishrāq, §235).

Around this text Mullā Ṣadrā develops a long discussion (Gloss 610, lithograph, p. 507) of the three levels of consciousness—sensory, imaginative, and spiritual—corresponding to the three degrees of being that constitute the human person: sensation, imagination, and spiritual intellection; body, soul, and Spirit.

Here he already sketches the idea of the soul's Miʿrāj, its ascent from the depths of mineral existence to the human form, through which, and together with which, it rises to the highest spheres of the spiritual hierarchies. This is a true ascent out of the Hells, the story of the Soul's metamorphoses until it reaches the world of human reality (ʿālam al-insānīya), the “human realm.”

From there it crosses the threshold of death and enters the Malakūt, the spiritual kingdom. A second and then a third growth mark the human being's destiny after death, each lasting through cosmic periods announced by the calls of Seraphiel's Trumpet (see Gloss 629 below). The ʿālam al-Mithāl belongs within this vision.
4. The World of Spiritual Imagination and the Resurrection Body

In Chapter III of Book V of the second part of the Oriental Theosophy, Suhrawardī deals specifically with the human being's destiny after death and the condition of souls once they have left the material body. Section 244 (see our edition, p. 229) considers those spiritual seekers who belong to the “intermediate” rank: they have attained perfection in inner purity, in “practical theosophy,” but have not reached perfection in Knowledge, or speculative theosophy.

In the classification of sages and spiritual seekers given in the Oriental Theosophy's prologue, these belong to the third category. “These souls,” writes the Shaykh al-Ishrāq, “escape into the world of self-subsisting Images and Forms, whose places of manifestation (maẓhar) are certain of the higher barzakhs”—that is, certain celestial bodies. “Their souls have the power to bring these spiritual Images and Forms (rūḥānīya) into existence (ījād) without a substrate.

“Thus they make present to themselves delicious foods, beautiful forms, exquisite sounds, and whatever else they desire. And these Forms are more perfect than those found in the world of our sensory experience. For the places of manifestation (maẓāhir) and supports of the latter are imperfect, being subject to decay, whereas the places of manifestation of the former are perfect.”

From these few lines Mullā Ṣadrā develops several essential aspects of his doctrine of Imagination (Glosses 613–616) and of the indispensable part it plays in any philosophy of resurrection. Without them, we are left with either the impossibilities of reading events of the world to come literally on the plane of physical sensation, or the emptiness of a rationalizing allegorical interpretation. In the last Gloss of this group, Gloss 616, Mullā Ṣadrā shows how his doctrine of imaginative consciousness belongs inseparably to the whole of his theosophy.

Taking up the idea of souls ascending after death from Heaven to Heaven—an idea our authors attribute to Plato and which is also expounded by the Ikhwān al-Ṣafāʾ, the “Brethren of the Pure Heart”—Mullā Ṣadrā first observes (Gloss 613, lithograph, p. 509) that these spiritual imaginal Forms, precisely because they are “suspended,” have no need of a material substrate in which to inhere. They require only the active subject that produces them (fāʿil). They subsist through the power of Imagination as the form of a work of art subsists through its artist, not as an accidental quality subsists in the substrate that passively receives it (qābil).
